demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
avoid anything that could be stressful
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I can no longer trust my own body
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette: Carlos Carlos, a 22-year-old HVAC technician of Latin American descent, has been struggling with the aftermath of an incident that occurred seven months ago. On April 15th, while working on an installation job in a commercial building, Carlos accidentally knocked over a ladder, causing his coworker to fall and suffer a severe injury. The memory of that day is etched into his mind like a nightmare, replaying the moment he hears any creak or sudden movement. Since then, Carlos has meticulously avoided anniversaries related to the event, such as April 15th and the days around it, fearing the flood of memories and guilt that would inevitably surface. He also avoids anything that might be stressful, leading him to cancel plans with friends and turn down new job opportunities, even though he needs them to support himself. The stressors have become so pervasive that he finds himself overanalyzing every detail of what happened, trying desperately to make sense of the accident and why it occurred. One of Carlos's primary fears is the feeling of being unsafe everywhere except in his home-a tiny apartment where he feels a semblance of security. When outside this safe zone, he is acutely aware that any unusual silence can trigger an overwhelming sense of impending danger. Recently, on several occasions, he felt his heart pounding and sweat breaking out when he heard a sudden quiet during work breaks or at night while walking home. The memory of the event feels alien to Carlos; it's as though someone else experienced it rather than him. This detachment is compounded by olfactory recall, where certain smells trigger memories of that day-smelling the dust in the air from his workplace brings back vivid images of the ladder falling and his coworker's screams. These intrusive memories force their way into his mind at random times, causing him to feel disoriented and disconnected from reality. Carlos's body has become unreliable to him; he can no longer trust its reactions or sensations, which he often interprets as signs of impending danger. He is haunted by the belief that he should have done more to prevent the accident, leading to a profound sense of guilt and shame. This inaction guilt has made it challenging for him to recognize himself as the same person he was before the event. The transformation feels so drastic that he sees his current self as someone entirely different. These symptoms have had significant consequences on Carlos's life. His reluctance to work beyond his home area has limited his opportunities, and he has turned down several job offers out of fear of similar incidents recurring. This avoidance behavior has also strained his relationships with friends who don't understand why he cancels plans last minute or seems distant when they spend time together. What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a recent incident where he had a panic attack at work, triggered by the smell of cleaning products that reminded him of the day of the accident. His coworkers were visibly concerned and suggested he talk to someone about what he was going through. Carlos is most afraid of never being able to forgive himself for his role in the accident but also hopes to find a way to reconcile with his past and regain control over his life. In therapy, Carlos has expressed a strong desire to understand how these symptoms developed and how they are interconnected. He wants to address his fears about trust and safety while learning coping strategies to manage his intrusive thoughts and physical reactions. Ultimately, he is hoping for a sense of peace and the ability to return to a life where he can work and socialize without constant fear and guilt weighing him down.
